column3: caveat

The reported failure moment M_t is NOT P x (tributary girt spacing) x L^2/8: the uniform line load per girt is taken as P/144 x (L_p x 12)/2 with L_p = 13.58 ft (half of the transverse panel span, = 81.48 in. of tributary width), even though the girts were spaced 7 ft out-to-out of web (p.21, Eq. 14).

M_t includes dead load: the panel weight term d_p/(w x 12 x 12) with d_p = 35 lb per 3-ft-wide panel and the girt self weight d_g/(L_g x 12) with d_g = 118 lb (Z8), 80 lb (Z10), 114 lb (C8), 78 lb (C10). Anyone recomputing moments from pressure alone will get ~0.3-0.5 k-in less (p.21).

R = M_t/(S_e F_y) in Appendix C uses the as-measured screw location C of that test; the C = B/2 normalised R-factors that are compared with AISI S100-07 appear only in Figures 42 and 43, not in the tables (p.29-31).

F_y is the average of three coupons (two flanges plus web) taken from an untested segment of the girt that actually failed; each test had two girts and generally only one failed, so the companion girt's properties are not reported (p.21).
S_e was computed with the commercial program CFS from measured midspan dimensions, not measured directly (p.21).

Screw location C was measured after failure as C = e + d/2, where e is the caliper distance from the pivot point to the hole edge averaged over the middle half of the span, and d is the screw diameter (0.182 in. for #12, 0.211 in. for #1/4-14) (p.23-24).
Fastener size changes with insulation thickness: 5 in. #1/4-14 screws for all 4 in. rigid-board tests, #12 for everything else; only test 13 (Z8B-2W) used a washer (p.23).
Panel thickness was 26 gauge throughout, but two panel profiles were used with very different yield stresses: D = 50 ksi, 1-1/8 in. rib; B = 80 ksi, 1-1/4 in. rib (p.21, p.49).
Specimen Z8D-1 failed by panel bending, so panels were stiffened at midspan for all 49 later tests; Z8D-1 therefore has no usable girt strength, no coupon F_y and no cross-section row (p.24, p.49).
In the rotational restraint section the same Cee specimens are named C250-1/C150-1 in Table 1 but C10-1/C6-1 in Tables 2 and 3; they are the same 10 in. and 6 in. deep specimens (p.5, p.10-12).

The web depth and the bare metal thickness were not varied independently: 8 in. girts are 0.100-0.102 in. thick and 10 in. girts are 0.059-0.061 in. thick, so 'depth effect' and 'cross-section slenderness effect' are confounded (p.21-22).

Failure loads in Table 3.3 / Table S1 are per linear foot of ONE purlin line, not the machine load: in the vacuum tests the manometer pressure (psf) is multiplied by the 5-ft purlin spacing (e.g. V2 = 229 lb/ft = 45.8 psf x 5 ft), and in the beam tests the footnote says the total span load divided by span length, while the load-rotation and load-strain figures are plotted as load 'on 2 purlins' up to 12 kips, implying the printed lb/ft is the machine load divided by two purlins and by the 20-ft span (B5: 280 lb/ft x 20 ft x 2 = 11.2 kips).

Test V1 is the only test with fixed (two-bolt, non-rotating) ends; all other tests were simply supported on rollers. Its 145 lb/ft is therefore not comparable with V5 (114 lb/ft) on the same purlin type A.
Test B2 re-used the purlin that survived test B1 and was 'badly distorted'; its 96 lb/ft is not an independent virgin-specimen result.
Yield and ultimate stresses in Table 3.1 are averages of three ASTM tensile coupons cut from lightly stressed regions of the FAILED purlin of each vacuum test, one set per purlin type, not per test.

Section dimensions in Table 3.2 are averages obtained by spray-painting a profile of an 18-in. cut length onto tracing paper and scaling the image; all section properties in the analyses were then computed assuming SHARP corners (justified because r/t > 4).

Test ultimate stresses in Table 4.1 are the last recorded strain before failure multiplied by E = 29500 ksi, i.e. elastic conversion; entries marked 'y' mean the gauge had yielded and no elastic stress is reportable.

Most purlins carried prepunched sag-rod holes near midspan and many buckles initiated there; the paper states that absence of these holes should give higher capacities, so these are 'as-supplied with holes' strengths.

The rotational restraint factor F is a secant value: the moment at the maximum large-scale test rotation divided by that rotation (the M-theta curve is nonlinear and F grows with rotation). F differs between the diaphragm-braced (vacuum) and channel-braced (beam) configurations for the same section.

Purlin type E was connected with self-drilling screws (the others with self-tapping screws into prepunched holes) and had negative initial sweep; its low strengths are confounded by both effects and the authors exclude it from several means.
Shear rigidity Q = 30 kips was measured on only two cantilever shear specimens, both halves of the vacuum test V3 assembly, with a panel framing detail that differs from Pekoz's earlier tests.
Failure load is the load at failure of the FIRST of the two purlins in the pair; the second purlin was often still intact (and in B4 was restrained by the testing machine column).

All roof-test loads are per purlin, in lb/ft (the figures are labelled 'UNIFORM LOAD PLF/PURLIN'); each test loaded two purlins at 5 ft 0 in. on centre with solid concrete blocks, so the 'uniform' load is a block-stack approximation over a 5 ft tributary width, not a true line load.

Table 1 gives one experimental value per test, which does not always equal the number annotated on the corresponding figure: Figure B.1 says 215 PLF where Table 1 says 214.5; Figure B.3 shows 219.5 PLF (west) and 198 PLF (east) and Table 1 lists 198.0, i.e. the governing (lower) purlin. Pooling must state which convention is used.

The 'Flexure/AISI' column is not an average: it is 1.67 times the SMALLEST of the four allowable uniform loads W computed in Appendix A from measured dimensions at each end of each of the two purlins (e.g. D-2: 1.67 x 144.447 = 241.2 lb/ft).
All Appendix A capacities and the Flexure/AISI predictions use the SPECIFIED yield of 70.0 ksi, not the coupon yields (75.2-79.5 ksi) of Table 2.
Coupon elongation is percent in a 2 in. gauge length and yield is 0.2% offset, per ASTM E-8-57T; only four coupons, one each from D-1 East, DI-2 West, DTB-4 and DTB-6.

The three shear-connector results (8,300 / 9,480 / 9,860 lb) are total testing-machine loads on a specimen with bridge sections on BOTH flanges (P = 2V in Figure 3); the authors quote the connector capacity as approximately 4,600 lb, i.e. about half the machine load. Do not pool the printed machine loads with per-connector capacities.
Purlin thickness is nominally 0.066 in. (ARMCO specification) but measured thicknesses in Appendix A run 0.064-0.070 in.; depth is nominally 8.05 in. with measured D4 from 7.90 to 8.16 in.
Part II reports data for only ten of the twelve Part I tests (D-1 to D-3, DI-1 to DI-3, DTB-3 to DTB-6); DTB-1 and DTB-2 appear nowhere in this volume.
The purlins were braced in a specific way (top flanges outward, opposing purlin counter-balancing roll, clip plates on the rafters); failure loads are not those of an isolated purlin.
Failure modes are not described in Part II; they are in Part I of the report.

P_u is reported as a line load in lb/ft on ONE purlin, not as a chamber pressure and not as a total specimen load: the footnote to Table 3 states P(lb/ft) = transducer reading (psf) x 76/2 x 1/12, i.e. the 76 in. wide chamber is split between the two purlins giving a 38 in. (3.167 ft) tributary width. Anyone pooling with psf-based datasets must multiply back by 3.167.

Each 'specimen' is a two-purlin assembly (north and south purlin, 5 ft apart, 20 ft long, span 237.5 in. between supports); Table 2 therefore has two geometry rows per test and the two purlins of one test are not independent specimens.
Load was applied and recorded in 5 psf increments (= 15.8 lb/ft), so P_u resolution is of that order.
Vertical deflections in Figures 8-10 were corrected for the simultaneous horizontal deflection of the purlin at each load increment; raw transducer data are not tabulated.
P_c' (unstiffened-flange computation) exists only for Z tests 1-4; P_c" (modified Cornell) exists only for tests 5-12. Empty cells in Table 3 are structural, not missing data.
Ratios in Table 3 are as printed; at least one (test 1, P_u/P_c' = 0.867 versus 123.5/140.5 = 0.879) does not recompute exactly from the printed loads.

Table 2 contains evident typographical anomalies (test 3 north B1 = 3.938 in. where all companion flanges are ~2.9-3.1 in.; test 5 south L2 = 8.813 in. where the companion value is 0.813 in.; test 9 south H = 7.063 in. where all other C webs are ~9.06 in.). Treat these as suspect before pooling.
Figure 10 is captioned 'Test No. 13' although only 12 tests were performed.
Section properties Ix and Sx (the Butler sheet, dated 8/10/83) are given only for specimens 5 through 12; specimens 1-4 have none.
Yield strengths F_y in Table 2 are per-purlin measured values but no coupon location, gauge length or test standard is reported.

Purlins were tested inverted (purlins on top) in a vacuum chamber with the tension flange screwed to the panel at 12 in. centres; panel profile, thickness and screw type are not identified beyond 'conventional roof panels' and 'self-drilling screws'.

All reported loads are per purlin in plf (pounds per linear foot of one purlin), not total machine or system load; gravity load was applied with 33 ± 0.1 lb concrete blocks in 33.0 plf increments, so load resolution is one increment.

Predicted failure loads in Table 3/Table 4 are AISI allowable moments multiplied by 1.67 (the implied factor of safety) with an ASSUMED yield stress of 56 ksi, not the measured 54.32 ksi average; test/predicted ratios are therefore slightly conservative by about 3%.
Each test had only TWO purlin lines; the 'external' purlin is the one farther from the lateral support joist and is the only one strain gaged, so stress data are from one purlin only.

Brace force percentages use two different normalisations: external brace forces are divided by the load supported by ONE purlin, internal brace forces by the load supported by BOTH purlins (two-purlin load).
Test V row in Table 8 is reported at 264 plf per purlin (its failure load), not 297 plf, because failure occurred below 297 plf.
Test IV rows in Tables 7 and 8 are NA because failure occurred at 127.1 plf, below 165 plf.
Test I is labelled I-2 and Test II is labelled II-3, indicating these were the second and third loadings of those setups respectively.
Diaphragm stiffness G' and Db' are reported only for the series average (Series A) and the single Series B test, not per individual test.
Tabulated purlin dimensions are measured, but section properties were computed by an AISI purlin analysis program using slightly rounded radii values.

Failure loads are per test purlin in pounds per linear foot (plf), not total chamber load: the vacuum pressure acts on a 5 ft tributary width (purlins at 5 ft on centre, Figure 1.4) and the reported value already includes the dead load of deck plus purlin (8.9 plf for 14 gage, 10.6 plf for Test 5 in 12 gage, 8.2 plf for Test 6 in 16 gage), e.g. Test 1: 140.63 plf applied + 8.9 plf dead = 149.5 plf (p. A.1, p. 26).

The 'predicted'/'reference' load in Tables 3.1 and 3.2 is the AISI constrained-bending, local-buckling capacity with the implied factor of safety of 1.67 removed (w_u = 1.67 x allowable), computed on an ASSUMED yield stress of 56 ksi, not on the measured coupon yield (average 54.05 ksi) (pp. 22, 23, 31).

The reference load quoted in Tables 3.1/3.2 is the w_u of ONE of the two interior test purlins (usually the one that failed), not the average or the minimum of the pair; Table 2.2 gives both purlins, which can differ by up to ~8% (e.g. Test 9: 174.2 vs 147.4 plf).

Only the two interior 9 x 3 C-purlins are 'test purlins'; the two edge 7 x 3 purlins are about 60% as strong/stiff and generally did not fail (pp. 1, 21). Capacities and section properties in Tables 2.1/2.2 (as extracted) are for the interior purlins only.
Spans are 25 ft 0 in. except Tests 15 and 16, which were 24 ft 8 in. (24.667 ft in the AISI runs); the reference loads for those two tests use the shorter span (pp. 2, A.61, B.84).

Material thickness is measured, not nominal: the west test purlin of Test 9 and both test purlins of Test 14 were about 0.010 in. thinner than nominal 14 gage (p. 13), which is why their reference loads are much lower.
Test 13 is not a valid strength result - the paper states it failed because of an error during construction of the setup (p. 23 note **, p. 30).

Table 1.1 and the narrative disagree on two configurations: Table 1.1 lists Test 10 intermediate braces as 'None' (wood stiffeners only) while Section 3.3 and Table 3.2 say bracing at ends and midspan; Table 1.1 lists Test 14 at 1/3rd points while Section 3.3 describes braces 2.5 ft each side of midspan.
Coupon results (Table 3.3) are from flat tensile coupons about 0.5 in. wide cut from failed test purlins; the gauge length over which the 27.9% average elongation was measured is not stated.
Deflections in Table 2.2 are given as in. per 100 plf for the stated span and are back-calculated from 5wL^4/384EI; the implied modulus is about 29,500 ksi (e.g. 29,793/I = Delta per 100 plf).

The 'torsional restraint' column of Table 1.1 is marked Yes only for Test 1 (where dynamometer braces at the rafters were measured); torsional restraint conduits were in fact installed at the rafters in most uplift tests (Figures 1.3, 1.4).

P_u is reported per purlin line, not as the machine/chamber load: the printed note on p.10 gives P(lb/ft) = transducer reading (psf) x 76/2 x 1/12, i.e. pressure times a 38 in. (3.167 ft) tributary width. Anyone pooling these data must not re-divide by the number of purlins.

Each test specimen contains TWO purlins (north and south), so Table 2 has two dimension rows per test number; a single thickness, Fy or lip angle cannot be assigned to a test without choosing or averaging the N and S values (Fy differs by up to ~2.5 ksi between the pair).
Span is 237.5 in. (19.79 ft) centre-to-centre of supports although the purlins themselves are 20 ft long; do not use 20 ft as the span.
Load was applied in 5 psf increments, equal to 15.8 lb/ft per purlin, so P_u resolution is of that order; P_u is the maximum pressure recorded by a pressure transducer at failure.

Mt/Mn in the 1987 LaBoube table is a re-analysis of the same 12 tests using the 1986 AISI Specification with Mn = Se Fy and Mt = w l^2/8; it is a different normalisation from P_u/P_c in the 1982 MRI table and the two must not be mixed as if independent tests.
The unbraced baselines quoted in the 1987 text (R = 0.50 for Z, R = 0.45 for C) come from outside this test programme and are not tabulated here.
Pc' (unstiffened-flange computation) exists only for tests 1-4 and Pc" (modified Cornell method) only for tests 5-12; the corresponding ratio columns are blank elsewhere and must not be read as zero.

Table 2 contains obvious transcription errors in the source (L2 = 8.813 in. for test 5 south, B1 = 3.938 in. for test 3 north, H printed as '9 7.063' for test 9 south); these should be flagged, not used as measured geometry.
Figure 10 is captioned 'Test No. 13' although only 12 tests exist; figure-to-test mapping should be treated with caution.
Self-weight of the inverted specimen is not stated to be added to or subtracted from the reported uplift loads.

Only four of the tests in this report are new: the two single-span base tests and two two-span continuous tests of Table 3.6/Table S1 (25 ft spans, 10 in. deep Z-purlins, rafter bracing). The thirteen tests of Table 1.1 are taken from the earlier Rivard and Murray project (FSEL/MBMA 86-01) and were not performed for this report.

All failure loads are uniform gravity loads expressed in plf (pounds per lineal foot) on a two-purlin-line system; moments are formed from that plf value as W L^2/8, so the plf is per purlin line, not a total machine or chamber load.
In Table 1.1 the span entry '3@23.0' means three continuous spans of 23.0 ft; the single-span entries are 20.0 ft. Table 3.6 spans are 25 ft and '2@25' means two continuous spans of 25 ft.

The measured failure loads of the two new single-span base tests are not printed as loads; they appear only as M_us in Table 3.7 (6688 and 7734 ft-lb), i.e. about 85.6 plf (rib) and 99 plf (pan) by W = 8M/L^2 with L = 25 ft (the 99 plf value is stated in the Appendix D sample calculation).
M_AISI in Table 3.7 is based on an assumed yield stress of 55 ksi (table footnote), not on coupon tests; the 8 in. purlins of Table 1.1 used a measured 56.6 ksi.
In Table 3.4 the columns headed 'Predicted' and 'Actual' are interchanged relative to Table 1.1: the first numeric column reproduces the experimental failure loads of Table 1.1.
Table 1.1 contains an apparent designation typo: the rib-panel, rafter-braced single span test is listed as 'P2/2-R-1' but is called R2/2-R-1 everywhere else in the report.
Deflections and brace forces in Tables 2.1 through 2.4 are at a nominal applied load of 40 plf, not at failure; the moments in Tables 3.5 and 3.7 come from stiffness analyses at a nominal 100 plf.

Rows flagged with an asterisk in Tables 3.3, 3.4 and 3.5 are declared 'not useful data' by the authors because the failure mode was not the predicted one; they should be excluded from any pooled correlation.
Purlin dimensions in the appendices are measured (per span, per purlin line) and the cross-sections differ slightly between the two purlin lines and between spans of the same test.

Failure load is per purlin line in lb/ft, computed from the manometer head as 2.7(10.4)(5.06) = 142.1 lb/ft and then REDUCED by the 8.5 lb/ft purlin+panel dead load, giving 133.6 lb/ft; the summary tables round this to 134 lb/ft while Attachment E prints 133.7. Anyone pooling must state which of 133.6/133.7/134 is used and must know the dead load has already been subtracted.

The manometer was read on one leg only (Attachment E column is headed '(ONE SIDE)'), so the factor 10.4 already contains a doubling of the single-leg reading; raw manometer inches cannot be converted to pressure with the usual 5.2 psf/in without this correction.

Only the two end-bay members that were instrumented/failed (A-3 and B-3) have measured yield strengths (54.5 and 55.0 ksi); the other four purlins in Table A have blank yield entries. Fy = 55.0 ksi used in all predictions is the B-3 coupon average, not a lot average for the whole assembly.

Table 1 lists the lap as '2-6' (2 ft 6 in., i.e. the total lap length across a support), whereas Attachment E and the drawing give '1'-3"/1'-3"' (1 ft 3 in. each side of the support). These are the same physical detail expressed two ways.
Thickness quoted for the test (t = .0681 in.) is the thickness of the failed member B-3, not an average of the six purlins, whose measured thicknesses range .0681–.0697 in.
Coupon gauge length is 2 in. (ASTM A370 sheet-type coupon, G = 2.00); elongations of 21.9–28.1 % are on that 2 in. gauge and are not comparable with 8 in. gauge values.

In Attachment D the third coupon of each member has a printed Y.P. stress that is not equal to the printed Y.P. force divided by the printed area (e.g. 1775 lb / .03501 in2 = 50,700 psi, but 56,412 psi is printed); the failure stresses are internally consistent. The reported averages (54,499 and 55,036 psi) were formed from the printed stresses.

The test is a direct duplicate of unbraced MBMA Continuous Span Test #3 except for the braces and the resulting zero initial sweep; Test #3 data in Tables 1 and 2 come from that earlier programme (different coil, Fy = 61.6 ksi, t = .0696 in.), so the braced/unbraced comparison is not thickness- or yield-matched.

Only the two end bays were braced; the centre bay bottom flange was unbraced, and both end-bay braces reacted against the side of the test box through double 2 in. rollers (not against a fixed, fully rigid point).

Axial loads are reported per purlin line, not per assembly: every test had TWO single-span purlin lines at 5 ft centres pulled together by one ram/load-cell chain through spreader beams, yet the tabulated failure loads (10-24 kips) are compared directly with STUDA2 capacities computed for ONE purlin. Anyone pooling the data must confirm the division by two before combining with single-member tests.

Uplift is not reported as a pressure: it is a line load in lb/ft per purlin obtained as (manometer inches of water) x 19.5 lb/ft/in for the 10 in. tests, or x 19.175 lb/ft/in for the 8 in. Z tests, PLUS the dead weight of the inverted roof system (5 plf for 8 in. Z, 7.6 plf for 10 in. Z, 9 plf for 10 in. C). The manometer was graduated only to 0.1 in. of water.

Because the chamber was inverted, a dead-load uplift moment of 6-8% of capacity is present even in the 'axial load only' tests; the quoted experimental axial capacity was therefore back-calculated through the interaction equation P = Pa(1-sqrt(M/Max)) and is not a directly measured pure-compression capacity.

Max is a nominal, not a measured, quantity: Max = R x 1.67 x (1986 AISI allowable flexural capacity from program AISIPROC), with R = 0.5 for single-span Z and 0.4 for single-span C, and factor of safety Omega_f = 1.0.

Pa in all tables is a computed value from Simaan's STUDA2 program, linearly interpolated between three computed capacities (weak/medium/strong rotational stiffness) using the measured AVERAGE screw location; it is not a measured capacity.
Spans in Table 3.3 for the three 7 in. C tests (17, 21, 25 ft) contradict Table 3.2 and the data packs (17, 19, 15 ft); Table 3.2 and the test summary sheets are the primary record.

Yield and tensile stresses come from one coupon cut at midspan from the WEB of each purlin that failed; coupon thicknesses in Table 3.5 differ by up to 0.009 in. from the measured thicknesses quoted in Table 3.2 and the data packs.

The 8 in. Z series (group A) has no STUDA2/CFS data because fastener locations were never recorded; its Pa (14.1 kips) was derived experimentally from test SP-8Z-0, and its fastener spacing was 6 in. rather than the 12 in. used everywhere else.

At least one calculation sheet (SP-10Z-12-3, 21 ft span) prints L = 300 in. in the M = wL^2/8 expression while the printed answer (5.0 in-k) corresponds to the correct 252 in.; check span-derived moments against the stated span.

Rotational stiffness F and allowable rotation FED come from 2 ft long cantilever purlin/deck specimens tested separately, with the fastener deliberately placed at strong, medium and weak positions; they are not measured on the full-scale assemblies.

All failure loads are uniform uplift loads expressed in pounds per lineal foot (plf) PER PURLIN LINE, not the total chamber load; the panel lengths and overhangs (1'-0" in the base tests, 2'-2 3/8" or 1'-9 3/4" in the multispan tests) were chosen so the vacuum pressure is distributed equally to each purlin line.

The paper reports two sets of failure loads for the same tests: Tables 3.2 and 3.3 give values about 5 plf higher (base tests) and 6-7 plf higher (multispan tests) than the Appendix data sheets and Table 4.1 (e.g. UZRP/S-1: 107.92 vs 102.92 plf; UCRP/S-3: 115.50 vs 108.52 plf). Only the Table 4.1 / Appendix values are consistent with the reported w_U3/w_P3 ratios.

Failure modes also disagree between sources: the Appendix data sheets call UZRP/S-1, UZRP/S-3, UCRP/S-1 and UCRP/S-3 'Local Buckle' while Tables 3.2 and 3.3 classify all rafter-braced-only tests as 'Distortional'. Table 3.2/3.3 classification should be used, as the text explains it (significant lateral deflection before failure).

Lap lengths in Table 2.1 are the TOTAL distance between the ends of the lapped purlins, not the distance between the web bolt lines, and the lap is not symmetric about the interior rafter (e.g. 66" = 40" + 26").
M_AISI in Table 4.1 is defined as the allowable moment capacity from the program 'Purlins' multiplied by 1.67 (i.e. nominal constrained bending strength S_eff x F_y), not an allowable value.

Yield stresses are coupon values (ASTM E8, 10-kip Instron) taken from the purlins that failed in each individual test; the base test and its confirming test have different F_y (e.g. 67.3 vs 64.2 ksi for UZRP/S), so base-test and multispan data should not be pooled on a single F_y.
The 1991 purlins for test sets UZRP/S and UZTR/F are about 0.01 in. thicker than the nominally identical 1990 purlins, so the 1990 and 1991 results for those two sets are not replicate pairs.

Table 4.1 prints w+_P3 = 368.8 plf for UCRP/S (O) 1991, whereas Appendix E computes 114.30 x 100 / 42.52 = 268.81 plf; the table value appears to be a typographical error (it does not affect w_P3, which is governed by the negative-moment equation).

UZTR/F-3 1991 ended in a deck buckling failure at the clips, not a purlin failure, so its w_U3 = 183.08 plf is a lower bound on purlin capacity and the paper deliberately reports no w_U3/w_P3 ratio for it.
The UZTR/F-1 base test data sheet says 'Pan Type Deck' while Table 2.1 and the UZTR/F-3 data sheet say Rib type; Table 2.1 should be taken as correct for the test set.

Component (simulated) test loads in Tables 4-1, 4-2 and 4-3 are PER SCREW = total actuator load divided by 2, because every component specimen carried exactly two fasteners (spacing 'F' = one screw in each outer valley; spacing 'C' = two screws in the centre valley). Do not pool the 'TL. LOAD' column with single-fastener data.

Standard Pullover Test loads (Tables 3-1, 3-3, 3-5, 3-7, 3-9) are the whole testing-machine load acting on ONE #12 screw through a 4.5 in x 12 in coupon, so no division applies; they are not comparable one-for-one with simulated loads.

Vacuum box (system) loads are individual load-cell readings under each screw, in pounds, with chamber pressure logged separately in psi; the 'Peak Loads' quoted in each test summary block are per failed cell, not totals.

Several time-history columns contain dead-instrument values (e.g. LCELL5 stuck near -808 lb, LCELL8 near -6000 lb after it was lost, LCELL2 inactive in Test 2). These must be filtered before any statistics are taken.

Panel thickness is reported as nominal gage in the test tables but as measured coupon thickness in Table 2-1 (26 ga Pascoe 0.021 in, 24 ga Pascoe 0.0234 in, 26 ga American 0.018 in, 24 ga American 0.022 in); the Chapter 7 calculations use t = 0.0239 in for 24 ga and 0.018 in for 26 ga.

Table 7-4 compares theory with REVISED means (outliers rejected by the Z test) for Pascoe 24 ga (1809 lb) and American 26 ga (1625 lb) but with raw means for Pascoe 26 ga (1654 lb) and American 24 ga (2123 lb).
Dean 26 ga data (Tables 3-9 and 4-3) come from earlier University of Florida research, not from this programme, and do not follow the same format or apparatus.
Reduction factors in Table 7-3 are the ratio of simulated capacity to Standard Test capacity for the same panel; the paper recommends the single lowest value (0.235), not the average (0.272).

The system tests used a 3.5 ft two-span arrangement, not the 5 ft purlin spacing of a real building; span was shortened deliberately to balance positive and negative moments and suppress panel buckling.

Each test used two purlins 5 ft apart in the 'opposed' position; only one of the two failed (usually the east member), and the single R value reported for a test comes from that failed member, not from an average of two.

The uniform uplift load on a member is NOT the chamber pressure: psf = manometer reading x 5.2, then the line load = psf x a tributary width of 4.27 ft (not the 5.0 ft purlin spacing), from which the panel dead load (1.2 psf) and the member dead load are subtracted before the moment is computed.

Table 1 'Tested Moment Capacity' is a back-computed simple-span moment (the paper never prints the failure load itself), and the 'Calculated Nominal Moment' uses the measured dimensions (Table A1) and measured yield (Table A2) of the failed member, so R is a measured-to-measured ratio, not a nominal-section ratio.

Member depths and thicknesses in Tables 1-10 are nominal/rounded labels; the measured web depth H in Table A1 (e.g. 6.40-6.45 in. for a '6.5 in.' member) and the 4-decimal thickness are the real values. Tables 2-10 round thickness to three decimals.

Rows labelled M1 and M2 in Tables 2-4, 6, 8-10 are proprietary manufacturer tests supplied to the author; for these only depth, span, thickness and R are given, with no moments, no failure modes, no material data, and no statement of panel type or insulation.
All insulation tests were on nominally 8 in. deep Z members only (3 in., 4 in. and 6 in. glass-fibre blanket); the insulation reduction factor r = 1 - 0.01t is extrapolated from that one group.
Table 12 mixes individual test rows with group 'Mean =' rows; the mean rows carry no test number and must be filtered out before statistics are recomputed.

Panels were 26 gage, measured 0.018 in. thick with 1.5 in. ribs at 12 in. o.c., and screws were placed ADJACENT TO THE HIGH RIB (the original AISI database used screws midway between ribs) - this screw position is the stated reason the new R values exceed the old ones.

The Appendix 2 deflection readings are ruler readings (decreasing numbers as the sheeting lifts), read to 1/100 in. by surveyor's level, not deflections; deflection must be taken as the change from the zero-load reading.
Coefficients of variation printed in Table 11 are inconsistent with mean and standard deviation (they appear to be variance/mean or similar); do not reuse them without recomputing.

W(tot) in Tables 1 and 2 is the line load carried by ONE purlin line (lb/ft), not the total chamber load: Mt (k-ft) = W(tot)·span²/8 /1000 reproduces every printed Mt exactly. Anyone pooling these loads must not divide again by the number of purlin lines.

Mn is computed as Se·Fy/12 (k-ft) from the effective section modulus and yield stress printed in the same row; no further strength reduction or overturning-moment effect is included (p.3: 'The Mt/Mn results do not include the effect of the overturning moment on the system due to the anchorage forces').

Fy = 55 ksi is printed for all eight Table 1 tests (apparently the nominal grade), whereas Table 2 lists measured coupon values 54.89-57.33 ksi; the two tables are therefore not on the same footing for Mn.
The symbol Se is used for two different things: effective section modulus (in^3) in Tables 1 and 2, and nominal shear strength of the eave member in the equation S_nt = S_n + S_e on p.7.

Tables 4 and 5 label their tests 1-8; these are the same specimens as 93-1 through 93-8 of Table 1 (Table 4 caption: 'for 8" Zee Tests in Table 1'), even though the purlins are 8.5 in. deep in Table 3.
The last column of Table 5 is headed 'lb' but its values are identical to the 'Uniform Load at Mt/Mn = 1.0, psf' column of Table 4; treat it as psf.
Failure load in psf (Tables 4 and 5) and W(tot) in lb/ft (Table 1) do not convert through a single stated tributary width; the implied width varies roughly 4.1-4.8 ft across tests.

Only tests 93-5 through 93-8 had the 1.5"x1.5"x0.12" continuous edge angle and the 6" high, 0.12" thick end clip; 93-1 through 93-4 had neither. The diaphragm was never anchored - it floated on top of the purlins.
The 36 lb/ft ultimate diaphragm capacity used to judge Tables 4 and 5 came from separate standard (cantilever) diaphragm tests on the same standing seam panels, not from the base tests.
The standing seam panel profile, clip type and manufacturer are not identified, so results cannot be transferred to another SSR system.

All failure loads are reported in plf (pounds per linear foot), i.e. a line load on a purlin line, not a chamber pressure; for the CECO tests the purlin spacing is 5 ft (Appendix cover page), so plf = psf x 5. Pooling with psf-based datasets requires this conversion.

The Virginia Tech loads in Table 1 are NOT the numbers printed in the original 1990/1991/1992 reports: the Introduction states the tributary area was computed in error and the failure loads were 'incorrectly reported', and Table 1 shows recalculated values.

For the CECO sets, the loads in Table 1 do not all equal the failure loads in the Appendix test summaries (e.g. SS2 66.6 plf in Table 1 vs 69.91 plf in the Appendix; SS3 128.1 vs 133.03; 3S5 129.2 vs 126.9). The basis of the difference (dead-load correction, re-reduction) is not explained; decide which value you are pooling.

Two of the six CECO sets failed in the connection/cladding rather than the purlin (SS4/3S4 clip failure, SS6/3S6 panel failure) and are flagged with asterisks; the paper's quoted range 0.63-1.15 and average 0.90 exclude them.
The body text says 'five sets of tests conducted by CECO Building Systems' while Table 1 lists six CECO sets; the average 0.90 is consistent with 13 sets (9 VT + 4 unflagged CECO).

Specimen detail for the nine Virginia Tech sets (section depth, thickness, span, panel and clip type) is not in this report; only the coded test designations (e.g. U-Z-R-P/S-1&-3) appear, and the data are in the cited CE/VPI reports.

All CECO purlins are Z-sections in the opposed orientation at 5 ft spacing on 30 ft spans; lap lengths are fixed by depth (8 in. Z: 0'-11 3/4" end bay, 1'-11 3/4" interior; 9.5 in. Z: 1'-5 3/4" and 2'-11 3/4").

Yield stress is sometimes reported as a single 'Avg. Yield' for the set rather than separately for purlin A and purlin B (SS1a, SS3, SS4, SS6, 3S1, 3S4, 3S6); a missing fy_B is not a missing material, it is a value not reported.
The predicted load is the minimum of a negative-moment-controlled and a positive-moment-controlled value (Eqs. 3a, 3b); which of the two governed each row is not reported.

The reported failure load is a line load on a single purlin line in plf, not a machine load: it equals 3.75 ft (assumed tributary width) multiplied by the chamber pressure in psf, plus an assumed purlin/panel self-weight (8 plf in five tests, 12 plf in FV20-3, where the summary sheet prints a minus sign but the arithmetic adds it).

Chamber pressure was read from U-tube manometers in inches of water and converted at 5.2 psf per inch in five tests (e.g. 12.9 in. -> 67.08 psf); in FV20-4 the printed conversion is 16.5 in. -> 82.5 psf, i.e. a factor of 5.0, so that test's psf value is inconsistent with the others.

Only one tensile coupon result is reported per test, machined from undamaged web material of the failed purlin; the thickness in Table 2.2 is a measured coupon thickness while the section designation (e.g. 8.5Z64) carries only the nominal thickness in thousandths of an inch.

Lap length is quoted as length INTO each bay (footnote to Table 2.1), so the total lap across an interior support is the sum of the two values (1.5 + 2.9 = 4.4 ft for the 20 ft tests, 1.5 + 3.5 = 5.0 ft for the 25 ft tests).

Mu, Vu and hence the unity checks in Table 3.1 were back-calculated from the recorded failure load by stiffness analysis assuming FULL continuity through the lap; they are not directly measured quantities.

The two 20 ft tests FV20-1 and FV20-2 differ from the rest of the population: purlin spacing 4 ft 11 in. (others 5 ft 0 in.), top flanges pointing OUT toward the chamber walls, anti-roll clips on the north line only and web stiffeners on the south line only; FV20-3 additionally used doubled screw-down panel. Chapter 2's blanket statement that all tests used opposed (inward-facing) purlins conflicts with the FV20-1/-2 summary sheets.

Only three of the six tests (FV20-3, FV20-4, FV25-1) actually failed in the intended shear-plus-bending mode outside the lap; the other three failed at supports and their failure loads are lower bounds on the shear-plus-bending capacity.

Each test comprised TWO purlin lines (north and south) with separate measured dimensions and separate Roof System Design capacity runs; the single failure load reported applies to the system, so a per-purlin-line attribution must be made by the user.

Load cells were placed under the exterior support in the west bay for the 20 ft tests but under the interior support (centre/west) for the 25 ft tests, so reaction plots are not directly comparable across the two span groups.
Stresses in the plots are not measured directly; they are measured strain multiplied by E taken as 29,500 ksi.

Loads are reported PER PURLIN LINE in pounds per linear foot (plf), not as a total chamber load: each test had exactly two purlin lines at 5 ft o.c. under a 7 ft wide panel with a 1 ft overhang each side (p.20, p.29).

The load was derived from a U-tube manometer reading (accuracy 0.1 in. of water; 1 in. water ~ 5.2 psf, p.21). Empirically the printed applied line load is a fixed multiple of the pressure: 19.50 plf per inch of water for the four Virginia Tech tests and 20.15 plf per inch for the three Ceco tests - i.e. an effective tributary width of about 3.75 ft and 3.88 ft respectively, which is neither the 5 ft purlin spacing nor half the 7 ft panel width. The paper does not state this conversion.

Table 3.2 reports APPLIED load only; the test summary sheets add 4.00 plf deck weight plus purlin self weight to give a 'Total Applied Load' (e.g. Test 1: 320.78 applied, 329.82 total, p.69). Chapter V says the 'experimental failure load' includes self weight, but the tabulated values do not follow this consistently (Test 1 is listed as 320.8, Test 2 as 142.4 where applied is 141.7 and total is 150.6).
I.P. Test 2's applied failure load is printed as 100.8 plf in Table 3.2 but as 102.8 plf in the summary sheet and in Tables 5.2-5.4 (p.38, p.141, p.65).

Yield stresses in Table 5.1 differ slightly from the coupon values in Table 3.1 (50.6 vs 50.0 ksi for Test 2, 87.5 vs 87.7 for Test 3, 75.0 vs 75.2 for Test 4); Table 5.1 values are the ones used in the strength predictions.
No coupon material was available for I.P. Test 3 Z-TF; its yield stress of 69.5 ksi is ASSUMED equal to the other I.P. tests and its tensile strength and elongation are blank (p.28).

Coupon gage lengths are not uniform: Test 1's coupon used a 2.000 in. gage length (37% elongation) whereas the remaining coupons used ~8.0 in. (10-22%). Elongations are therefore not directly comparable (p.75 vs pp.90, 104, 120, 135).
I.P. Test 3 'through fastened' panel is the same standing seam pan panel screw-fastened directly to the top flange, not the through-fastened panel used in Tests 1 and 4 (p.60, p.16).
Anti-roll clips were placed at every support for the Z-purlin tests but only at the EXTERIOR supports for the C-purlin tests (p.17).

Spread (bottom-flange roll) was measured about 2 in. above the bottom flange, 1 ft each side of the CALCULATED inflection point and at the calculated maximum-moment point; only the test bay was instrumented, and no measurements were taken in non-test bays (pp.21, 24).
Lb in Table 5.1 is the distance from the END OF THE LAP to the theoretical inflection point in the test bay computed by a non-prismatic stiffness analysis, not a measured length (p.55, p.76).
R factors (0.44/0.45) for the standing seam systems come from the AISI Base Test Method performed elsewhere, not from these tests; R is set to 1.00 for through-fastened panel (p.51, p.55).

Axial failure loads in Table 1 are loads per purlin pair? No — Table 1 lists the machine/assembly failure load, but note the assembly contains two purlins; the text reports for A1 'Failure load = 62.1 kips' for the two-purlin assembly while Table 1 lists 31.1 kips, i.e. Table 1 is the per-purlin load (assembly load divided by two). Anyone pooling these data must apply the per-purlin convention.

Table 5 'Axial Load' is NOT the raw test load: it is the raw per-purlin load first corrected to an equivalent pure axial load via an interaction equation using strain-gage-derived bending moments, then multiplied by 0.75 to remove the weak-axis end fixity supplied by the bolted end-plate loading beams. A1: 31.05 kips raw -> 33.2 kips interaction-corrected -> 24.9 kips after the 25 percent reduction.

Axial stress in Table 5 uses the gross unreduced area; bending stress in Table 5 uses an EFFECTIVE section modulus. k_af therefore mixes a gross-area axial stress with an effective-section bending stress.

Flexural results F1-F4 are pre-existing manufacturer base-test data, not tests run by the authors; only the four axial tests were newly conducted. Diaphragm stiffness and rotational stiffness of those assemblies were never measured, only approximated.

Specimen depths and thicknesses quoted in the assembly descriptions are nominal (e.g. 0.120 x 2.5 x 8.5); measured values in Table 4 differ (e.g. A3 t = 0.095 in. against a nominal 0.100 in., A4 t = 0.060 in.).
d/t used in Tables 8 and 9 and in the proposed design equations is computed from measured depth and thickness of the FLEXURAL specimen (F1-F4), not the axial specimen.
The 512 finite element rows in Appendices 2 and 3 are numbered up to 576; 64 numbers (5-8, 13-16, ... 125-128) were deleted as outside practical limits, so test numbers are non-contiguous.
Corrected FEM stresses are truncated at 18 ksi axial and 35 ksi flexural, so many corrected k_af values are the artefact 18/35 = 0.514 rather than a computed ratio.

FEM k_af pairs an odd-numbered axial model with the following even-numbered uplift model; the uplift entry reports a TOTAL uplift load W (kips), not a stress, and the flexural stress is computed as wL^2/8 divided by the gross section modulus.

The reported 'Total Applied Load' is a line load per purlin line (plf), not a chamber pressure or a per-area load: the summary sheets convert the measured pressure differential at about 19.5 plf per inch of water (5.20 psf/in. H2O acting on roughly a 3.75 ft tributary width per purlin), then add 4.00 plf deck weight and the measured purlin self weight.
Rt as tabulated is a LOAD ratio (total applied load / equivalent line load); because span and loading pattern are identical it equals Mts/Mnt, but anyone pooling moments must not re-divide.

The overturning term 2PL(d/B) of Eq. 2.1 was deliberately omitted from all Chapter IV / Chapter V Rt values; the authors state its inclusion would raise every value 6%-8%. However, the first six Appendix A summary sheets (30 ft span, insulated, Tests 1-6) DO contain a 'Ridge Purlin Correction' line in the total load, so those rows are not on the same basis as the rest.

Mnt = Set x Fyt uses MEASURED cross-sectional dimensions (Set from the Virginia Tech C/Z program, E = 29,500 ksi) and the MEASURED yield stress of the failed purlin (two web coupons, ASTM A370, 0.2% offset, ~8 in. gage length), not nominal properties.

Series 1 is heterogeneous: five tests at 25 ft span with no insulation plus six tests at 30 ft span with 6 in. metal building insulation, even though Table 4.1 lists Series 1 as 25'-0" with no insulation.
Series 4 (four tests) is excluded from the report entirely; the 118 tests come from Series 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 and 10.

Clip nomenclature drifts between appendices: C1 appears as 'Low, Sliding'/'Short, Sliding'/'Low, Floating', C2 as 'Low, Fixed'/'Short, Fixed', C3 as 'High, Sliding'/'High, Floating'/'Tall Sliding'. The series identifier (-C1/-C2/-C3) in the test ID is the reliable key.
Flange width is not printed on the summary sheets; it must be taken from Table 4.1 (nominal 2 1/2 in. or 3 1/2 in.) or from the measured-dimension drawings accompanying each test.
Only the governing purlin (eave or ridge, as stated in the failure-mode line) is used for the section properties and Fy, but the load reported is the common per-purlin chamber-derived line load.
